title: BRAIN-QA and ingest

story: The owner of the CI page in the brain, our repo of short pages about how our systems work, tidies it on a quiet Friday. The new title is "Pipelines overview", and the text now uses the team's newer words: backend pipelines trigger on each commit, the dashboard pipeline triggers on pull requests. Every sentence is still true. Lint is green, a teammate approves, and the page is merged.

The next week, three people ask the brain's Slack bot whether frontend CI runs when they push to their branch, and three times it answers "I don't know". The page is still there and still right. Search simply cannot find it any more, because none of the words people actually type, "frontend", "CI", "push", are left on it. Nothing failed, so nobody noticed.
hook.question: How do we notice, before the merge, that an edit made the brain worse at answering the questions people really ask?

read.h: A test made of real questions
p: Code has tests; the brain needs one too. Ours is called BRAIN-QA, and it is a golden set: a fixed list of inputs with known good answers, run again after every change, like a regression suite for a component. The inputs are 60 questions that people really asked in public engineering channels in the last six months, not questions we invent, because invented questions use the words of the people who wrote the pages and are always easy to find.

Each case names the page or pages that answer it, and two to four answer points a correct answer must contain. About six questions have no page yet, and for those the right answer is "I don't know" plus where to ask; they test that the brain does not make something up. The questions are spread over cloud, client, frontend, CI, product, decisions and runbooks, and tagged, so a drop in one area shows up by name.

code.text:
id: bq-017
question: "When I change a proto in fcp_common, what do I need to do so old on-prem clients keep working?"
asked_in: public          # private questions are rewritten as a summary
source_pages:             # any of these in the top 5 of kb search counts as a hit
  - engineering/cloud-client-compatibility.md
  - engineering/code-run-path.md
answer_points:            # a judge checks each point; all must be there for "correct"
  - "Protos live in common/fcp_common/rhinoAgentRpc/ and the generated _pb2 files are committed (make protoc)"
  - "Add new fields instead of renaming or removing old ones, because installed clients still use them"
  - "Cites at least one page as rnd-kb/<path>@<sha>"
expect: answer            # answer | not_in_kb
tags: [be, cross-tier, protos]

notes.text: Close to the words a person really typed. That is what makes the test honest.
Retrieval is right when any of these pages is in the top 5 of kb search.
Answer points are checked one by one, so "mostly right" is not "correct".
not_in_kb cases expect an honest "I don't know".

p: The first measure is cheap: for each answerable question, run the same kb search that people and Nova use, and check whether a source page is in the top 5. That is called a retrieval hit, and the share of hits is the retrieval score. It needs no model call, it takes seconds, and it gives the same result every time, so it can run on every pull request in rnd-kb as a step of the lint job.

The target is at least 85%, and a pull request below it fails. That is exactly the check the tidy CI page needed: two questions drop out of the top 5, the score falls, and the owner learns before merging that the page must keep the words people search with. The step prints only case ids and totals, never the question text, because CI logs are visible to everyone who can see the repo.

notes.text: not_in_kb cases have no page to find, so they are left out of this score.
The same search() the kb CLI uses. Testing a different ranking would prove nothing about Nova's.
A hit means a page that really answers the question, not just any result.

p: A test only means something if the thing being tested has never seen it. If a question and its answer were written into a brain page, search would find that page easily and the bot would repeat the answer, and the score would measure memory instead of knowledge. Machine-learning people call this a leak.

So the cases never live in rnd-kb. They sit in a restricted repo for evaluation data that agents and the bot cannot read, and the runner reads them with the brain's GitHub App. A second check catches the leak that a person causes by accident, such as pasting a Slack question into an FAQ page: it breaks every question into runs of 8 consecutive words and fails if any run appears in any page. Eight words is long enough that it almost never happens by chance.

notes.text: Every window of 8 words: a question of 12 words gives 5 runs.
Spaces around each run, so a run cannot match in the middle of a longer word.

p: Finding the right page is necessary but not enough; the answer must also be right. So every night the runner asks each question for real: through claude -p with the kb plugin (Sonnet 5.5 at low effort) at first, and through the Slack bot's own answer function once the bot exists, so the score measures what people get. A judge, Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort, marks each answer point PASS or FAIL, and an answer is correct only when every point passes. The target is 80% correct.

A judge is a model too, so before anyone trusts it, it is compared with a person's own labels on 10 answers. The nightly job runs on the agents' runners and reaches Claude only through our LLM gateway with an evals key, so the runner holds no Anthropic key.

Pages also go stale when code changes and nobody updates them. Every Monday, a script, kb ingest-collect, lists the fcp pull requests merged and the Jira epics closed since the last run, and matches each one to the pages whose applies_to globs or sources it touches. Changes that match no page go into a separate list as candidates for new pages. The script makes no model calls, so finding the news is cheap and repeatable.

Then a routine (the same agent code as Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, but started by a schedule instead of a ticket) reads that list on a small VM and updates only the pages with news, opening one pull request per page owner. It may edit page bodies and add sources, never raise confidence above med, and never touch DATA-SCOPE.md, OWNERS.yml, the templates or the workflows. It starts in shadow mode, where its proposed changes are only saved and compared with what an owner would write.

lab.title: Catch an edit that hides an answer
lab.goal: Score retrieval over a small golden set, watch a harmless-looking edit fail it, and add the leak check that keeps the test honest.

guess.q: Five answerable questions. After an edit, two of them no longer find their page in the top 5. What is the retrieval score, and does the pull request pass the 85% target?

options.why: 3 of 5 hits is 60%, well below 85%, so the check fails before the merge.
Retrieval does not ask whether the page exists, but whether search finds it for the question.

options.text: 50%, because the not_in_kb question counts as a miss
options.why: not_in_kb questions are left out of retrieval: there is no page to find.

follow.say: Write the search. It is the same BM25 you built in the search lesson, as one function that returns the ranked page paths.
Write the scorer. It runs search() for each answerable question and checks that a source page is in the top 5.
follow.do:
cat > brain_qa.py <<'EOF'
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

from search import search

TARGET = 0.85


def retrieval(cases: list[dict], kb_dir: str) -> tuple[float, list[str]]:
    answerable = [c for c in cases if c["expect"] == "answer"]
    missed = []
    for case in answerable:
        top5 = search(kb_dir, case["question"], limit=5)
        if not any(page in top5 for page in case["source_pages"]):
            missed.append(case["id"])
    return 1 - len(missed) / len(answerable), missed


def main() -> None:
    cases = [yaml.safe_load(p.read_text()) for p in sorted(Path(sys.argv[1]).glob("*.yaml"))]
    score, missed = retrieval(cases, sys.argv[2])
    print(f"cases: {len(cases)}  missed: {', '.join(missed) or 'none'}")
    print(f"retrieval: {score:.0%} (target {TARGET:.0%})  {'PASS' if score >= TARGET else 'FAIL'}")
    sys.exit(0 if score >= TARGET else 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
EOF
uv run --python 3.13 --with pyyaml python brain_qa.py golden/cases rnd-kb

lab.build: Add the leak check to brain_qa.py: import tokens from search, add word_runs(text, n=8) that returns every run of 8 consecutive words, and leaked(cases, kb_dir) that returns the ids of cases with any run found in the pages. Print leaked: <ids or none> and exit with 1 when anything leaked. Then plant a leak, as a helpful person might: create rnd-kb/runbooks/faq.md with a title in its frontmatter and the line "Why are my integration tests stuck waiting for the QA lock? See the QA lock runbook." Run the scorer: retrieval still says PASS, but leaked: bq-002 and exit=1. Delete faq.md and run it again.
checks: The tidy edit makes the scorer print missed: bq-003, bq-004 and retrieval: 60%, and exit with 1.
The better wording brings retrieval back to 100% while keeping "Pipelines overview" on the page.
With faq.md in place, the scorer prints leaked: bq-002 and exits with 1, even though retrieval passes.
After deleting faq.md, it prints leaked: none and exits with 0.
You can explain why bq-006 is not part of the retrieval score.

solution.text:
# at the top: also import tokens
from search import search, tokens


def word_runs(text: str, n: int = 8) -> list[str]:
    words = tokens(text)
    return [" ".join(words[i : i + n]) for i in range(len(words) - n + 1)]


def leaked(cases: list[dict], kb_dir: str) -> list[str]:
    pages = " " + " ".join(" ".join(tokens(p.read_text())) for p in Path(kb_dir).rglob("*.md")) + " "
    return [c["id"] for c in cases if any(f" {run} " in pages for run in word_runs(c["question"]))]


# in main(), after the retrieval line
    leaks = leaked(cases, sys.argv[2])
    print(f"retrieval: {score:.0%} (target {TARGET:.0%})  {'PASS' if score >= TARGET else 'FAIL'}")
    print(f"leaked: {', '.join(leaks) or 'none'}")
    sys.exit(0 if score >= TARGET and not leaks else 1)

check.q: An owner rewrites a page in new words. Every fact is still true and lint is green. How can BRAIN-QA's retrieval check still fail?

options.text: It cannot: if the facts are right, the brain answers correctly
options.why: The facts are only useful if search finds the page. With the readers' words gone, real questions stop finding it.

options.text: The questions people ask no longer bring the page into the top 5 of kb search
options.why: Retrieval measures what readers experience: whether their own words lead to the page that answers them.

options.text: The judge marks the new wording as wrong
options.why: Retrieval uses no judge and no model at all. It only runs search.

check.q: Someone suggests storing BRAIN-QA's questions in rnd-kb "so they are next to the pages". What goes wrong?

options.text: The questions become part of what search and the bot read, so the test measures memory instead of knowledge
options.why: Search would find the questions' own text, and the bot could repeat the stored answer. The score would rise without the brain getting better.

options.text: Nothing, as long as the folder is named tests/
options.why: Search reads every markdown page in the mirror, and the bot reads the whole repo. A folder name does not hide anything.

options.text: The lint would fail because the cases have no owner
options.why: Even with owners, the problem is that the brain can see its own test.

check.q: Why do the not_in_kb questions matter, if they are left out of the retrieval score?

options.text: They make the retrieval score look better
options.why: They are excluded from retrieval, so they cannot change it.

options.text: They are mistakes in the golden set waiting to be removed
In the nightly answer run they check that the bot says "I don't know" and where to ask, instead of making something up
options.why: A brain that answers everything confidently is dangerous. These cases reward an honest "I don't know".

p: BRAIN-QA is 60 cases under brain-qa/ in the restricted golden-set repo (the same repo as TICKET-BENCH's data), about six of them not_in_kb, each with source_pages, two to four answer_points and tags; private-channel questions are rewritten as summaries and names are removed. rnd-kb-tooling/evals/brain_qa.py has --mode retrieval, a step in kb-lint's CI that reads the cases with the rhino-kb App and prints only ids and totals, failing below 85%, and --mode answers, nightly on the agents' runner set through the LLM gateway's evals key: claude -p with the kb plugin until the bot ships, then the bot's answer(). The judge is Sonnet 5.5 at medium, checked against Shai's labels on 10 answers; results go to the eval store as JSON, with the two numbers in the check summary. The leak check fails on any 8-word run of a question in a page, or if the golden-set repo is in any search or bot source list.

kb ingest-collect searches merged fcp PRs and, with read-only JQL, epics moved to Done since --since (given by the Temporal schedule, so the script keeps no state), and writes work.json per page plus an unmatched list, keeping titles and links only. The kb-ingest charter (ai-agents/routines/charters/kb-ingest.yaml) runs it every Monday on a lite VM under routineRun with the kb and pr-story skills, pushes only kb-ingest/<week>/<owner> branches in rnd-kb, keeps confidence at most med, stays in shadow for two weeks, and follows the routines' noise rules (one open PR per owner, closed after 7 idle days).

tickets.why: The 60 real questions with source pages and answer points, kept where the brain cannot read them.
The runner: retrieval on every rnd-kb PR, judged answers nightly, and the leak check.
kb ingest-collect: this week's merged PRs and closed epics, grouped by page.
The kb-ingest routine that opens page-update PRs for owners.

words.plain: A fixed list of inputs with known good answers, run again after every change to catch regressions.
Our golden set for the brain: 60 real questions with the pages and points that answer them.
The share of answerable questions whose source page is in the top 5 of kb search.
When test questions or answers end up where the tested system can read them, so the score measures memory.
A model that marks each answer point PASS or FAIL, checked first against a person's labels.

review.q: What does a BRAIN-QA case contain, and what is each part for?
review.a: The real question; source pages (a hit if one is in the top 5); answer points (all must pass for correct); expect answer or not_in_kb; tags to see which area dropped.

review.q: Why is retrieval cheap enough for every PR while answers run nightly?
review.a: Retrieval runs only the search code, with no model calls, in seconds and deterministically. Answers need a model to answer and another to judge, which costs money and time.

review.q: How does the leak check work, and why 8 words?
review.a: It breaks each question into runs of 8 consecutive words and fails if any run appears in a page. Eight words almost never match by chance, but a pasted question always does.

remember: Test the brain with real questions it has never seen: check on every change that search still finds the answering page, and keep the questions where the brain cannot read them.
